title: The ADHD bathroom reset that actually gets done
description: An ADHD bathroom cleaning reset that actually gets done: a five-minute wipe-and-go in a fixed order, tied to your shower. No deep clean, no decisions.
h1: Why the bathroom never gets cleaned with ADHD (and the five-minute reset that fixes it)
target_query: ADHD bathroom cleaning reset that actually gets done

faq.q: How often should I clean the bathroom with ADHD?
faq.a: Do the five-minute reset twice a week, tied to a shower you already take, and stop planning a deep clean at all. Two short resets keep a bathroom presentable indefinitely. If it has been a while, the first reset just takes ten minutes instead of five, and then you are back on the twice-a-week rhythm.

faq.q: Why is cleaning the bathroom so hard when it's such a small room?
faq.a: Because a bathroom is a small room with a lot of separate surfaces, and each surface is its own start. Sink, taps, mirror, toilet, floor, shower: that is six tasks pretending to be one, and starting tasks is the part ADHD makes expensive. A fixed order removes the starting problem by making each step the automatic next move.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to make a bathroom look clean?
faq.a: Clear the counter and wipe the sink and taps. A clear counter and a shiny tap read as clean to anyone walking in, even if the shower has not been touched. If you have ninety seconds, do those two and nothing else.

sources.supports: Task initiation and planning deficits explain why a room made of six small separate jobs stalls before it starts.
Altered time perception in ADHD is why the bathroom feels like an hour-long job when it takes five minutes.
External cues and fixed sequences substitute for weaker internal self-regulation, which is why tying the reset to the shower works.
